path.summary: SQL is fifty years old and refuses to die because it is the cheapest way to ask a precise question of a lot of data. This course gives you the mental models that make queries readable instead of memorized: tables as spreadsheets with rules, JOINs as set theory, GROUP BY as a controlled collapse. By the end you can read unfamiliar SQL, write queries that scale, and spot the named traps before production does.

blocks.md:
SQL is the second-most-popular language in the world (after JavaScript) and has been for thirty years. Its grammar predates the iPhone. The 50-year-old syntax is the *feature*, not the bug — every analyst, every founder, every PM you'll ever work with reads the same dialect.

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to write a query that asks a precise question of a lot of data, without scrolling through Excel. That's the entire job, distilled.

blocks.title: Mental model: spreadsheets with rules
blocks.md:
A SQL table is a spreadsheet that signed a contract.

- Every column has a **fixed type** (int, text, date, money). Excel lets you mix; SQL doesn't.
- Every row is the **same shape**. No skipping columns. No surprise extras.
- Most tables have a **primary key** — one column whose values are unique. That column is how the database finds a row in microseconds.

This is why SQL holds a billion rows and your spreadsheet chokes at one million. The rules are the speed.

blocks.caption: Watch the same data drift in Excel vs hold its shape in SQL across 100,000 inserts.

hi-IN.title: VLOOKUP ke jail se baahar
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, tu Excel mein VLOOKUP karke jail mein hai. 50,000 rows pe file open hone mein 30 second lagta hai. Cell type randomly change ho jaata hai — phone number mein '+' lag jata hai, date column 'general' ho jata hai.

SQL mein same query: `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id = 42` — **15 milliseconds. Even on 50 million rows.** Speed difference is not 100x; it's literally a different category of tool. Excel ek nautanki hai, SQL ek railway hai.

en.title: From the Excel jail
en.md: Excel chokes at a million rows. SQL doesn't blink at a billion. The same lookup that takes 30 seconds in Excel takes 15 milliseconds in SQL, on 1000x more data. Not an optimization — a different category of tool.

blocks.text: Move 1 — SELECT, FROM, WHERE in plain English

blocks.md:
Every SQL query is a sentence. Read it left to right and translate:

```
SELECT  name, city          ←  these columns
FROM    customers           ←  from this table
WHERE   city = 'Mumbai'     ←  where this is true
```

In English: *give me the name and city of every customer in Mumbai*. The order matches your question. Once you see this, you cannot un-see it.

blocks.prompt: Run this query and read the result. Then change the WHERE clause to find only customers from Pune.
blocks.hint: Only the WHERE value changes. The shape stays the same.

blocks.title: Translation moment: 'show me Bengaluru customers who signed up after April'

steps.label: 1. English
steps.body: Show me Bengaluru customers who signed up after April.

steps.label: 2. The grain
steps.body: We are asking about customers, one row per customer. So FROM customers.

steps.label: 3. The columns
steps.body: We want their identity and signup date. SELECT name, signed_up_at.

steps.label: 4. The filter
steps.body: Two conditions joined with AND: city is Bengaluru, and signed_up_at is after 2024-04-30.

steps.label: 5. The full query
steps.body: Read top to bottom; English question maps to SQL grammar.
steps.code:
SELECT name, signed_up_at
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Bengaluru'
  AND signed_up_at > '2024-04-30';

blocks.prompt: Which clause filters which rows are returned?

choices.label: WHERE
choices.explain: Correct. WHERE evaluates a condition per row and keeps the rows where it's true.

choices.label: SELECT
choices.explain: SELECT picks which COLUMNS appear in the result. It does not filter rows. Common confusion.

choices.label: FROM
choices.explain: FROM picks which table you're querying; it doesn't filter rows.

choices.label: ORDER BY
choices.explain: ORDER BY sorts rows that already passed the filter; it doesn't drop any.

hi-IN.title: SELECT * = production mein bug
hi-IN.md:
Tu jaldi mein hai. `SELECT * FROM orders` likh diya. Kaam ho gaya, ship kar diya.

Day 30: kisi ne `orders` table mein ek `internal_notes` column add kar diya — full credit-card numbers logged karne ke liye. Tera report ab in numbers ko Slack pe email kar raha hai. Compliance team ko notification gaya hai.

**`SELECT *` is a bug waiting for a column to be added.** Always list columns. Discipline jail nahi hai; future-tu ke liye favor hai.

en.title: The SELECT * bug-in-waiting
en.md: `SELECT *` is a bug waiting for someone to add a column to your table. The day they add `internal_notes` containing PII, your harmless report becomes a compliance incident. List your columns. Always.

blocks.text: Move 2 — Always pick columns; never SELECT *

blocks.md:
**`SELECT *`** is the most common anti-pattern in SQL. It looks innocent — *give me everything!* — but it has three problems:

1. **Schema drift.** When someone adds a column to the table, your query silently picks it up. If the new column contains sensitive data, you've leaked it.
2. **Performance.** Wide tables can have 50+ columns; you almost never need all of them. Reading them all costs network and memory.
3. **Readability.** The next person reading your query has no idea what you actually use. Listing columns is documentation.

The rule: **list every column you use, every time.** It's two extra seconds; it's a permanent rebate.

blocks.caption: Same query intent, two shapes. The left one accepts whatever the table grows; the right one accepts only what you asked for. Auditing a query of the second kind is mechanical.

scenarios.explain: Clean. Specific columns, specific filter, no anti-patterns.
Anti-pattern: `SELECT *`. List columns. Schema drift will eventually leak data through this query.
Subtle bug. Standard SQL uses single quotes for string literals; double quotes are interpreted as identifiers in some databases (Postgres) and would error. Replace with single quotes.

scenarios.situation:
```sql
-- comment: get all customer data for the report
SELECT * FROM customers;
```
scenarios.explain: Comment claims intent ("all customer data for the report") but the query is `SELECT *`. The report wants 4 columns, not the 18 in the table. List them; the comment is then redundant (the SELECT IS the comment).

blocks.title: The classic trap: 'SELECT * for now'
blocks.md:
You're prototyping. You write `SELECT *` to see what's in the table. Then you copy that query into the production code. Then someone adds a column. Then you have a leak.

**'For now' is the most expensive phrase in software.** List the columns the moment you know which ones you need. Two extra seconds, infinite peace of mind.

blocks.prompt: Order these steps to translate 'top 3 cities by customer count' into a query you'd ship:

items.label: Identify the grain: one row per CITY (not per customer)
items.detail: We want a city-level result, so the output is grouped.

items.label: FROM customers — that's our source
items.detail: The detail is at the customer level; we'll aggregate up.

items.label: GROUP BY city, then COUNT(*) AS n
items.detail: Aggregation collapses the customer rows into one row per city.

items.label: ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 3
items.detail: Sort by count, take the top 3. Now we have the answer.

blocks.instruction: Write a query against the customers table that returns the name and signed_up_at of every customer in Pune, sorted most recent first. List the columns; do NOT use SELECT *.
blocks.expected:
SELECT name, signed_up_at
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Pune'
ORDER BY signed_up_at DESC;

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO TRUE statements about basic SELECT queries:

choices.label: ORDER BY runs after WHERE — sorting only happens on rows that already passed the filter
choices.explain: Correct. We'll cover the full execution order in lesson 5; for now, remember: filter, then sort.

choices.label: Listing columns explicitly is more maintainable than SELECT *
choices.explain: Correct. Schema drift, performance, and readability all point the same direction.

choices.label: Single quotes and double quotes are interchangeable for string literals
choices.explain: False in standard SQL and most databases. Single quotes for string literals; double quotes are for identifiers (column names, table names) — and many databases reject the mixing.

choices.label: WHERE city = NULL filters to rows where city is missing
choices.explain: False. NULL is the absence of a value; you cannot equal something that isn't there. Use `IS NULL`. (Covered properly in lesson 2.)

hi-IN.title: Mummy ke ration list ka SELECT
hi-IN.md:
Mummy ration list banaati hai. Pucha *"sab kuch likh do"* — pura kitchen lika ja sakta hai. Tu *"daal-chawal-aata sirf"* bola — focused list mili.

Mummy `SELECT *` nahi karti, kabhi nahi. Specifically asks. Tu kyun karta hai? **Discipline same hai. Domain alag.**

en.title: The grocery-list test
en.md: When you ask for a grocery list, you say 'rice, dal, oil' — not 'everything in the kitchen'. Why is your SQL different? Same discipline; different domain.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The SELECT * That Leaked PII
blocks.source: Anonymous backend engineer at Tatva Health, a Bengaluru-based series-B health-tech startup
blocks.story:
On August 14, 2024, Tatva's growth team launched a new partner-referral dashboard. The query powering it was, charitably, *seven days old*: `SELECT * FROM patients JOIN referrals ON ...`. It worked beautifully on staging. Three weeks later, on September 3, the schema team added a column called `aadhaar_last_four` to the `patients` table — a perfectly reasonable addition for a new KYC flow.

Nobody changed the dashboard query. Nobody had to. The `*` happily picked up the new column and started piping it into the partner portal — a portal that **42 external referral partners** could log into.

The leak was caught 11 days later by a security review, not by the engineering team. Internal post-mortem put exposed records at **₹0 in fines** (caught before reporting threshold) but **18 engineering-days** of cleanup, partner notifications, and a board-level memo. The fix was four characters: replacing `*` with the explicit column list the dashboard actually needed.

The engineer who wrote the original query had been at the company eight weeks. The reviewer who approved the PR had been there four years.
blocks.takeaway: `SELECT *` is not a shortcut — it's a contract you didn't read with a schema you don't yet have.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The 4PM Friday Customer List
blocks.setup:
It's 4:07pm on a Friday. **Aanya, your PM**, walks up to your desk holding her laptop like a tray. *"Just a quick one — can you pull me the customer list? I need it for a partner call at 9am Monday. Should be five minutes, right?"*

The office is emptying. Your weekend plans involve a Goa flight at 7am tomorrow. The `customers` table has 19 columns. You have one shot to do this right before the Friday-night brain-fog sets in.

coach.name: DBA Aunty Lakshmi
coach.role: Senior database administrator, 18 years on call so you don't have to be

stages.prompt: Aanya hovers. You open your SQL client. What's your **first move**?

options.label: `SELECT * FROM customers;` — fastest, send the CSV, catch the flight.
options.explain: Aunty Lakshmi raises one eyebrow. The `customers` table has 19 columns including `password_hash`, `aadhaar_last_four`, and `internal_risk_score`. You just emailed all of it to a PM who will forward it to a partner. Friday-evening dread incoming.

options.label: Ask Aanya: "Which columns do you actually need, and is this for an external partner?"
options.explain: **Correct.** Two questions, ten seconds, saves your weekend. Aanya thinks for a moment and says: *"Oh — name, city, signup date. And yes, it's going to a partner."* You just dodged a PII incident.

options.label: Pull `SELECT * FROM customers LIMIT 100;` and let Aanya filter columns in Excel.
options.explain: Limiting rows doesn't limit columns. The 100-row sample still contains every sensitive field, and now there's a CSV with `aadhaar_last_four` sitting in someone's Downloads folder forever.

options.label: Say "can't do it, raise a ticket" and go home.
options.explain: Aanya escalates to your manager, who finds someone who *will* run `SELECT *`. You skipped the work but didn't prevent the incident. Partial credit only because you didn't personally cause the leak.

stages.prompt: Aanya confirms: **name, city, signup date, external partner**. You write the query. Which version ships?

options.label: `SELECT name, city, signed_up_at FROM customers;`
options.explain: **Clean.** Three named columns, one table, zero surprises. If marketing adds a `lifetime_value` column tomorrow, this query won't quietly start leaking it.

options.label: `SELECT name, city, signed_up_at FROM customers WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;`
options.explain: **Even better.** You filtered out soft-deleted accounts — a partner doesn't need to see customers who asked to be forgotten. Aunty Lakshmi nods approvingly.

options.label: `SELECT name, city, signed_up_at, email FROM customers;`
options.explain: Aanya didn't ask for email. You added it because "they might need it." That's how scope creeps into a partner data dump. Email is PII the partner has no consented basis to receive.

options.label: `SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 1=1;` and delete the columns in Excel.
options.explain: The `WHERE 1=1` does nothing. The `*` does everything. The Excel filter doesn't exist in the CSV download you just emailed.

stages.prompt: Query runs. 47,000 rows. CSV exports in 8 seconds. Aanya is reaching for the file-attachment button. **Last call** — what do you say?

options.label: "Looks good, send it. Have a great weekend!"
options.explain: Aanya emails 47,000 customer records as an unencrypted CSV attachment. It bounces off the partner's 25MB Gmail limit, gets re-sent via WeTransfer, and lives on a public link for 7 days. You technically did your job. Aunty Lakshmi sighs.

options.label: "Drop it in the secure-share folder, set 7-day expiry, send Aanya the link — not the file."
options.explain: **This is the move.** Link beats attachment. Expiry beats forever. The partner gets what they need, the audit trail is clean, and on Monday at 9am Aanya looks like the most prepared PM in the room.

options.label: "Send only the first 100 rows so the partner can sample, then we'll do the rest later."
options.explain: Now Aanya has to chase you on Monday for the full file, from her partner call, while you're 30,000 feet over Karnataka. You optimized for your weekend, not the outcome. Half-measure.

options.label: "Hold up — let me also add a row count and the run timestamp so we can audit this later."
options.explain: **Solid.** A one-line comment header (`-- 47,231 rows · 2026-05-08 16:14 IST · pulled by you for Aanya · partner: Acme Co.`) takes 5 seconds and makes the next post-mortem (if there is one) trivial.

outcomes.perfect: Flawless. You scoped the request, wrote the minimum-viable query, shipped it via the right channel, and left an audit trail. **Aunty Lakshmi pours you a virtual filter coffee.** Now go catch your flight.
outcomes.good: Good instincts on most of it — you avoided the headline disaster. Re-read the lesson on `SELECT *` semantics before next Friday's last-minute request, because they always come back.
outcomes.learn: You shipped data you didn't need to a channel you shouldn't have used. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **explicit column lists** and **why `*` is a contract**. The good news: this was a drill. The next one might not be.

blocks.md:
Most SQL bugs that ship to production are filter bugs. Not the obvious kind. The kind where the query *runs successfully*, returns 4,200 rows that look correct-ish, and silently misses 600 because of a NULL that doesn't compare the way you assumed.

By the end of this lesson, you'll know exactly how WHERE evaluates each row, how NULL pollutes your filters, and how to write conditions that mean what you wrote.

blocks.title: Mental model: three-valued logic
blocks.md:
Most languages have two truth values: true and false. **SQL has three: TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN.** Whenever a condition involves a NULL, the result is UNKNOWN — not TRUE, not FALSE.

WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. UNKNOWN rows are dropped, just like FALSE rows. They look identical from your seat. They are not the same thing.

This is the source of more silent bugs than any other feature in SQL. Memorize the three values; treat NULL with respect.

blocks.caption: Watch a query run row by row, with the truth-value lighting up TRUE / FALSE / UNKNOWN — and the silent rows that get dropped.

hi-IN.title: Mummy se 'kuch laaya?' — three valued logic
hi-IN.md:
Tu ne ghar pe milk laana tha. Mummy puchti hai *"laaya?"*

- **TRUE** — "haan laaya" — milk fridge mein
- **FALSE** — "nahi laaya" — daant padti hai
- **UNKNOWN** — *answer skip kar diya, phone dekhne laga* — Mummy ne assume kiya nahi laaya. Aaj khichdi banegi.

SQL same hai. Silence (NULL) `false` ke saath dropped hota hai. Tujhe lagta hai filter ne work kara, actually 600 rows silently chale gaye. Mummy thi toh chai ban jaati. Yahan toh production bug.

en.title: The 'silence is no' problem
en.md: You don't answer mom's 'did you bring the milk?' Silence ≈ no. Same in SQL: a NULL in your filter condition produces UNKNOWN, which gets dropped just like FALSE. The row 'looks like' it failed your test. It didn't fail; it never got tested.

blocks.text: Move 1 — Operators that do what you mean

blocks.md:
Operators in SQL look like the operators in your other language. They mostly behave the same. The two places they don't:

- **Equality**: `=` and `<>` (or `!=`). Standard. Don't use them on NULLs (more on this in Move 2).
- **Range**: `BETWEEN x AND y` is **inclusive on both ends**. So `WHERE amount BETWEEN 100 AND 200` includes rows where amount is exactly 100 and exactly 200.
- **Set membership**: `IN (a, b, c)` is the clean way to say 'one of these'. Avoid long `OR` chains.
- **Pattern match**: `LIKE 'A%'` matches strings starting with A; `LIKE '%a%'` matches strings containing a. `_` matches a single character. Slow on big tables — index can't help on a leading wildcard.
- **NULL test**: `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`. Never `= NULL`.

hi-IN.title: WHERE the cat sat on — IN ka bhula chhoda
hi-IN.md:
Tu likhta hai:
```sql
WHERE city = 'Mumbai' OR city = 'Pune' OR city = 'Bengaluru' OR city = 'Chennai'
```

Four ORs. Tedious. Bug-friendly — agar fifth city add karni ho toh fir copy-paste, fir typo, fir 2 baje raat ko on-call.

**Use IN. Always.**
```sql
WHERE city IN ('Mumbai', 'Pune', 'Bengaluru', 'Chennai')
```

Kam likhna, kam bug, parser bhi khush.

en.title: OR-chain anti-pattern
en.md: Three or more `OR` conditions on the same column? You wanted `IN (...)`. The `IN` form is shorter, harder to typo, and reads like English. Convert any OR chain longer than 2 the moment you write it.

blocks.text: Move 2 — NULL is not a value

blocks.md:
**NULL means *unknown* or *missing*.** It is not zero. It is not empty string. It is the absence of a value.

The consequence: any operator applied to NULL returns NULL (UNKNOWN), not TRUE or FALSE. So:

- `WHERE city = NULL` — *never* true. Returns zero rows. Bug.
- `WHERE city = 'Mumbai'` — drops rows where city is NULL even though those rows are clearly *not* Mumbai. The row failed silently.
- `WHERE city <> 'Mumbai'` — also drops rows where city is NULL. Even more surprising.

The fix: use `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` for NULL tests, and **explicitly handle NULLs in non-equality filters** when missing rows are valid answers.

blocks.title: The classic trap: WHERE-the-cat-sat-on
blocks.md:
Senior SQL writers call this *the WHERE-the-cat-sat-on bug*. The cat (NULL) was definitely on the mat, but your filter didn't see it because you assumed equality would touch every row.

Whenever you write `<>` or `NOT IN` or `NOT LIKE`, **explicitly decide what should happen to NULLs**:

- *NULLs should be excluded* (default behavior): leave it.
- *NULLs should be included*: add `OR <col> IS NULL` to your condition.

Do this in writing, not in your head. Future-you will thank present-you for the comment.

hi-IN.title: COALESCE — NULL ka 'default value' fix
hi-IN.md:
Indian forms pe yeh dekha hai? *"If not applicable, write N/A"*. **COALESCE** SQL ka same hai.

```sql
SELECT customer, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city
FROM orders;
```

NULL ki jagah `'Unknown'` aa jaati hai. Filter mein bhi use kar sakte ho:
```sql
WHERE COALESCE(city, '') <> 'Mumbai'
```

Dangerously simple, dangerously useful. Do not use to *hide* NULL bugs — use to *handle* them explicitly.

en.title: COALESCE — the explicit-default tool
en.md: `COALESCE(col, default)` returns the column value, or the default if the column is NULL. Use it to make NULLs explicit, not to hide them. The rule: declare your treatment of missing values, don't accept whatever the database happens to do.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The NULL That Failed an Audit
blocks.source: Anonymous data engineer at PaisaPe, a Mumbai-based payments series-C
blocks.story:
PaisaPe runs settlement reconciliation every night for ~14 million transactions. On March 11, 2025, the RBI auditor for their quarterly review pulled their internal "failed-payment" report and found a **0.42% discrepancy** versus the bank's own statement: ₹4.7 crore of transactions that the bank said happened, that PaisaPe's own report said didn't.

The culprit was one line in a query that had run, untouched, for 19 months:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM transactions
WHERE payment_status <> 'success'
AND created_at >= '2024-12-01';
```

The problem: when an upstream service timed out, it wrote `NULL` into `payment_status`. And `NULL <> 'success'` doesn't evaluate to `TRUE`. It evaluates to `NULL`. Which the `WHERE` clause treats as "don't include this row."

Result: **62,400 timed-out transactions** had been quietly excluded from every "failed payments" report for 19 months. The auditor noticed because the bank's reconciliation file included them. The fix was eight characters: `OR payment_status IS NULL`. The remediation memo to RBI was twelve pages.

The engineer who wrote the original query had left the company in 2023. The query had passed code review three times.
blocks.takeaway: `NULL` is not equal to anything, not even itself — and `WHERE x <> 'A'` silently drops every row where `x` is unknown.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The Missing 1,400 Customers
blocks.setup:
It's Tuesday morning. **Aanya, the same PM from Friday**, is back. *"Quick one — the customer-segmentation report says we have 8,600 active customers in Tier 2 cities. But the marketing dashboard says 10,000. Where are the missing 1,400?"*

She's on a call with the CMO in 40 minutes. The two queries were written by two different engineers, one of whom is on parental leave. You crack open both queries.

stages.prompt:
Query A (segmentation, 8,600) reads:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers
WHERE tier <> 'Tier 1' AND tier <> 'Tier 3';
```

Query B (marketing, 10,000) reads:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers
WHERE tier = 'Tier 2';
```

What's your **first hypothesis**?

options.label: Query B is wrong — it's missing some Tier 2 variants like 'tier 2' or 'TIER_2'.
options.explain: Possible but unlikely — Query B is the *more inclusive* count. Case mismatches would make it *smaller*, not bigger. Aunty Lakshmi gestures at the screen impatiently. Look at Query A again.

options.label: Query A excludes rows where `tier IS NULL` — those 1,400 customers have a NULL tier.
options.explain: **Spot on.** `NULL <> 'Tier 1'` is `NULL`, not `TRUE`. Same for the second clause. Both fail, the row is excluded. Query B's `tier = 'Tier 2'` *also* excludes NULLs — but Query B is the one that's correct *for marketing's intent* (only count confirmed Tier 2).

options.label: Query A and B are both correct — the difference is timing; one ran before a backfill.
options.explain: Both queries were run at the same hour. The discrepancy is structural, not temporal. Aunty Lakshmi reminds you: *"NULL is the first thing you check when two counts disagree."*

options.label: There's a JOIN somewhere fanning out one of the counts.
options.explain: Both queries are single-table `COUNT(*)` from `customers`. No JOINs, no fan-out. Read the queries again — the difference is in how `WHERE` treats NULL.

stages.prompt: You confirm: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE tier IS NULL` returns **1,400**. Aanya needs to know which number to give the CMO. **What do you tell her?**

options.label: "Use 10,000. Query B is right; Query A has a NULL bug."
options.explain: Half-right. Query A *does* have a NULL bug. But "Tier 2" customers and "customers with no tier yet" are not the same business segment. The CMO will plan a campaign for 10,000 people, then 1,400 of those targeted folks will get an offer for a tier they don't actually have.

options.label: "Both are technically correct for what they ask. The real number depends on what the CMO means by 'Tier 2': confirmed-Tier-2 (8,600) or not-classified-as-non-Tier-2 (10,000). Ask her."
options.explain: **This is the answer.** The bug isn't the count — it's the ambiguity. Aanya goes back, asks the CMO, returns 90 seconds later with: *"Confirmed Tier 2 only."* You ship 8,600 and add a NULL-tier follow-up to the next sprint.

options.label: "Use 8,600 — it's the more conservative number."
options.explain: Conservatism is not a substitute for correctness. The CMO might *want* the 1,400 unclassified customers in the campaign — those could be the highest-intent new signups. You're choosing for her without telling her.

options.label: "Average them: 9,300. Splits the difference."
options.explain: Aunty Lakshmi physically winces. Averaging two counts is never an answer to a data question. Please do not put this in the deck.

stages.prompt: The CMO says **"confirmed Tier 2 only."** You ship 8,600. Aanya asks: *"How do we make sure this NULL-mismatch never happens again?"* What's the **best long-term fix**?

options.label: Add a `NOT NULL` constraint on `customers.tier` and backfill the 1,400 NULLs to a default like 'Unclassified'.
options.explain: **The right move.** Constraints prevent the ambiguity from re-entering the system. Backfilling NULLs to an explicit `'Unclassified'` label means future `WHERE tier <> 'Tier 1'` queries actually count those rows. Three-way decisions become two-way decisions.

options.label: Write a wiki page reminding everyone that `<>` ignores NULLs.
options.explain: Wiki pages do not enforce SQL semantics. The next engineer to write `tier <> 'X'` will not have read your page. Documentation is a backstop, not a fix.

options.label: Add `OR tier IS NULL` to every existing query as a one-time sweep.
options.explain: You'd need to find every query, in every dashboard, in every notebook, in every cron job. You will miss some. And the next engineer will write the bug all over again.

options.label: Ban `<>` from the codebase via a SQL linter rule.
options.explain: Banning operators is a hammer where you need a constraint. `<>` is fine; ambiguous data is the problem. Aunty Lakshmi says: *"Fix the schema, not the syntax."*

outcomes.perfect: You diagnosed a 19-month-old class of bug, refused to ship a wrong number under time pressure, and proposed a fix that prevents the next incident. **Aunty Lakshmi adds you to her short list of people she'll answer at midnight.**
outcomes.good: You found the NULL. You shipped a number. The fix you chose was a backstop instead of a structural prevention — re-read the section on three-valued logic and constraints, because this exact bug will reappear.
outcomes.learn: Re-read the lesson on `NULL` semantics — especially **"NULL is not equal to anything, not even itself"** and the section on `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. The CMO is now planning a campaign for the wrong customer set. Tomorrow you'll have to walk it back.

points: SQL has three truth values: TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN — WHERE keeps only TRUE
NULL means 'unknown'; any operator applied to NULL returns NULL (UNKNOWN)
Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for NULL tests; never `= NULL`
Negative filters (`<>`, `NOT IN`) silently drop NULLs — handle them explicitly
COALESCE is the canonical fix when you want NULL to be treated as a known default

lessons.title: JOINs Are Just Set Theory With Tables
lessons.subtitle: INNER, LEFT, and the fan-out trap

audioChapters.label: Opening — the moment SQL gets useful
Move 1 — INNER vs LEFT, picked by intent

blocks.md:
Until now, we've worked with one table at a time. Real questions almost always span tables: *which customers ordered in March?* (customers + orders). *Show me each order with its product name* (orders + products).

JOINs are the operator that links tables. They are also where 60 percent of all 'wait, why are there suddenly 50,000 rows?' production incidents come from. By the end of this lesson, you'll pick the right JOIN by intent and never accidentally fan out a row again.

blocks.caption: Watch the JOIN engine match rows from the customers table to rows from the orders table — and see what survives each JOIN type.

blocks.title: Mental model: JOINs are matchmakers
blocks.md:
A JOIN takes two tables and produces a new wider table by **matching rows on a key**. Different JOIN types differ only in *what to do with the unmatched rows*.

- **INNER JOIN**: only matched rows survive
- **LEFT JOIN**: all rows from the left, plus matches from the right; unmatched right side becomes NULL
- **RIGHT JOIN**: same in reverse (rarely used; usually rewrite as LEFT)
- **FULL JOIN**: everything from both; unmatched on either side becomes NULL

The key to picking is asking: *what should happen to a row that doesn't match?* That answer chooses the JOIN.

blocks.prompt: Click each join type to see exactly which rows survive. Notice the orphan order 104 (no customer) and the customer 4 with no orders.

hi-IN.title: Mumbai junction — JOIN ka real-world
hi-IN.model:
Mumbai-Dadar junction socho. Western line ki train (left table) Central line ki train (right table) se milti hai.

- **INNER JOIN** — woh passengers jo dono trains pakad rahe hain — minimum, but high-confidence interchange.
- **LEFT JOIN** — pure Western line ke passengers + jo Central pakad sake, woh extra info. Western waale skip nahi honge.
- **FULL JOIN** — sab passengers, kisne kaunsi train pakdi, kuch ne dono.

JOIN type teri intent ke saath match karna chahiye, **station ke layout ke saath nahi.**
hi-IN.md:
Picture Mumbai's Dadar junction. Western Line trains (left table) and Central Line trains (right table) meet there.

- **INNER JOIN** — only passengers who caught BOTH trains. Minimum, high-confidence interchange.
- **LEFT JOIN** — every Western Line passenger, with the Central Line info if they caught it. Western passengers don't get dropped.
- **FULL JOIN** — every passenger from either line, with a NULL where they didn't take the other.

The JOIN type matches your *intent*, not the platform layout.

en.title: The interchange-station analogy
en.md: Two train lines meet at a station. INNER JOIN keeps only passengers on both lines (sparse, high-confidence). LEFT JOIN keeps everyone from one line, optionally annotated with their other-line info. The choice is about which group you don't want to lose.

blocks.text: Move 1 — Pick by intent, not by syntax habit

blocks.md:
When you write a JOIN, ask one question: *what's the unit of work — what shape do I want my output to be?*

- *I want a list of customers, with order info if they have any* → LEFT JOIN customers → orders. Customers without orders still appear (with NULLs).
- *I want only the customer-order pairs that actually exist* → INNER JOIN.
- *I want orphan orders too — orders where the customer has been deleted* → LEFT JOIN orders → customers (note the direction reversed).

**The unit of work is the table on the LEFT in a LEFT JOIN.** That's how you think about it.

blocks.code:
-- 'List of customers with their lifetime order count (zero is fine)'
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- 'List only customers who have placed at least one order'
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

choices.label: INNER JOIN products → orders
choices.explain: Drops products with zero sales — exactly the rows you said you wanted.

choices.label: RIGHT JOIN products → orders
choices.explain: Same effect as INNER for this question; the orders side has no orphan products to bring back.

choices.label: FULL JOIN
choices.explain: Brings back orphan orders (orders for deleted products) — you didn't ask for those, and they'll inflate your count.

hi-IN.title: Customers + orders ka dimaag-fryer
hi-IN.md:
Junior dev pucha — *"customer ka name aur order amount chahiye, sab customers ke liye, even agar koi order nahi hai."*

Junior likhta hai:
```sql
SELECT c.name, o.amount
FROM customers c, orders o
WHERE c.id = o.customer_id;
```

**Comma JOIN!** Yeh implicit INNER hai. Customers without orders silently dropped. Junior ko lagta hai *"output theek lag raha hai"* — half ki list missing.

Fix: explicit LEFT JOIN. Comma-JOIN bhul ja, ek baar mein. Yeh 1990s ka code style hai.

en.title: Comma-JOIN is dead — use LEFT JOIN
en.md: The `FROM a, b WHERE a.id = b.fk` style is implicit INNER JOIN — and it silently drops the unmatched rows the junior wanted to keep. Use explicit LEFT/INNER JOIN syntax. The 1990s wrote comma-joins; we don't have to.

blocks.md:
Here's the failure mode that ships to production every week somewhere on Earth.

You JOIN customers to orders. Customer Aanya has 5 orders. Suddenly Aanya appears 5 times in your result, with each of her orders. Now you SUM her revenue and it's correct. Or you AVERAGE her age and it's wrong — *each Aanya row got counted again*.

This is the **fan-out trap**: a JOIN multiplied a row in the unit-of-work table by the number of matches in the joined table. Aggregations downstream then double-count.

The fix: **either pre-aggregate the right side before joining, or use COUNT DISTINCT carefully.**

blocks.title: The classic trap: fan-out
blocks.md:
Whenever you JOIN to a table with multiple matches per row, **the left side gets multiplied**. Aggregations on left-side columns silently double-count.

Diagnostic: if your COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) doesn't match the number of customers in the JOIN result, you've fanned out. Fix:

1. **Pre-aggregate the right side** in a CTE (covered in lesson 5):
   ```sql
   WITH order_summary AS (
     SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
     FROM orders
     GROUP BY customer_id
   )
   SELECT c.name, c.age, COALESCE(s.total, 0) AS total_revenue
   FROM customers c
   LEFT JOIN order_summary s ON s.customer_id = c.id;
   ```
2. **Use COUNT(DISTINCT)** when you can't pre-aggregate easily.

coach.name: DBA Aunty Lakshmi
coach.role: Has audited a thousand fan-out incidents

intro: Beta. Three queries. Each has a bug or a smell. 🔍
Each is from a real PR I've reviewed. The names are changed; the bugs are not.

scenarios.situation:
```sql
SELECT c.name, AVG(c.age) AS avg_age
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
```
scenarios.explain: Fan-out. Each customer row is multiplied by their order count, so AVG(c.age) is weighted by orders, not by customers. If Aanya has 5 orders and everyone else has 1, her age dominates the average. Fix: aggregate orders in a CTE first.

scenarios.situation:
```sql
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
```
scenarios.explain: Correct. SUM is fan-out-safe (sums multiplied rows still produce the right total). COALESCE handles customers with zero orders. GROUP BY c.id (the primary key) is the disciplined form.

scenarios.situation:
```sql
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.amount > 1000;
```
scenarios.explain: NULL bug + bonus issue. The WHERE on `o.amount > 1000` silently turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN — it filters out the rows where o.amount is NULL (i.e., customers with no matching orders). If you wanted *all customers, with a flag for high-spend orders*, move the condition into the ON clause: `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.amount > 1000`.

scenarios.situation:
```sql
SELECT c.name, COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
```
scenarios.explain: Correct. COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) is fan-out-safe; the DISTINCT prevents a multi-counted match from inflating the count. For a customer with no orders, o.id is NULL and COUNT skips it (count = 0).

scenarios.situation:
```sql
SELECT p.name, AVG(o.amount) AS avg_order
FROM products p
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.product_id = p.id
INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name;
```
scenarios.explain: Correct. The aggregation is on `o.amount`, which lives at the order grain — JOINing to customers does not fan out *orders*, only adds annotation. AVG is fine here.

blocks.prompt: Order these steps to debug a query that returns way more rows than expected:

items.label: Count distinct primary-key values vs total rows in the result
items.detail: If they differ, you've fanned out somewhere.

items.label: Identify which JOIN duplicated rows by removing one JOIN at a time
items.detail: Bisection — find the offender quickly.

items.label: Pre-aggregate the offending right-side table in a CTE before joining
items.detail: The standard fix; collapses many rows to one before they multiply the left side.

items.label: Verify aggregations are on columns that survive the fan-out (SUM, COUNT DISTINCT) — not weighted aggregates (AVG of left-side columns)
items.detail: Last check; ensures the result is what you actually meant.

  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.id, c.name, COALESCE(t.total, 0) AS total_revenue

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO TRUE statements about JOINs:

choices.label: A WHERE filter on a right-side column of a LEFT JOIN can silently turn it into an INNER JOIN
choices.explain: Correct. `WHERE o.amount > 0` drops rows where o.amount is NULL, including the unmatched LEFT JOIN rows. Move conditions into the ON clause if you want them to apply only to the JOIN match.

choices.label: SUM and COUNT(DISTINCT col) are fan-out safe; AVG of a left-side column is not
choices.explain: Correct. SUM tolerates duplicates (the math still adds up). AVG of left-side columns is weighted by the right-side row count — almost always wrong.

choices.label: RIGHT JOIN is functionally equivalent to LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped
choices.explain: Correct, but as a style point — most teams write everything as LEFT JOIN to keep mental model consistent. RIGHT JOIN is rarely seen in modern code.

choices.label: An INNER JOIN never produces NULLs in the result
choices.explain: False. INNER JOIN drops unmatched rows but the surviving rows can still have NULL values in their original columns (from the source data, not from the JOIN itself).

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 3x Revenue That Wasn't
blocks.source: Anonymous analytics lead at Kettlebell Fitness, a Pune-based D2C wellness brand
blocks.story:
Two days before Kettlebell's series-A board meeting, the marketing team produced a slide titled **"Q3 Revenue by Acquisition Channel."** The headline number: **₹14.2 crore**, up 47% QoQ. The board was thrilled. The CFO was confused.

The CFO's own ledger said Q3 revenue was **₹4.8 crore**.

The analytics team had built the slide off this query (paraphrased):

```sql
SELECT channel, SUM(orders.amount)
FROM customers
JOIN attribution_touchpoints USING (customer_id)
JOIN orders USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY channel;
```

The `attribution_touchpoints` table had, on average, **2.9 rows per customer** — every Instagram ad, every Google search, every newsletter click. The JOIN multiplied each order by every touchpoint. Customer Aanya, who had 3 ad touches and bought ₹2,500 worth of kettlebells, contributed **₹7,500** to the revenue total. Across 18,000 customers, the inflation came out to roughly **2.96x** — close to the 3x miss.

The slide was killed at 11pm the night before the board meeting. The CEO called the analytics lead personally. Nobody was fired, but trust in the marketing dashboard took **6 months** to rebuild — the team instituted a mandatory "pre-aggregate before joining" review for any cross-domain query.
blocks.takeaway: JOINs multiply rows; aggregations downstream double-count — pre-aggregate the many-side first, or you'll ship a number 3x too big.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Customers With Order Counts
blocks.setup:
It's a Wednesday standup. **Aanya is back** — *"For the customer-success team, I need a list of every customer with their order count. All customers, even ones who haven't ordered yet, because success wants to reach out. By lunch please."*

The schema:

```sql
customers (id, name, city, signed_up_at)
orders    (id, customer_id, amount, status, ordered_at)
```

A customer can have zero, one, or many orders. You have one query to write.

stages.prompt: First decision: **which JOIN type** gets you "all customers, including ones with zero orders"?

options.label: `INNER JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id`
options.explain: INNER drops customers with no matching order row. The 1,200 customers who signed up last week and haven't bought yet — exactly the people success wants to call — vanish from your result. Aunty Lakshmi shakes her head.

options.label: `LEFT JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id` with `customers` on the left.
options.explain: **Correct.** LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table (`customers`) and fills NULL for any unmatched right-side columns. Zero-order customers come through with NULL in the order columns — exactly what success needs to find them.

options.label: `RIGHT JOIN customers ON ...` because the customers list is the priority.
options.explain: A `RIGHT JOIN` keeps everything from the *right* table. You wrote `customers` on the right of `RIGHT`, so this technically works — but it's a readability disaster. Aunty Lakshmi: *"Always lead with LEFT. Future-you will thank present-you."*

options.label: `FULL OUTER JOIN` to be safe.
options.explain: FULL OUTER also keeps orphan orders (orders whose customer was deleted). You don't want those in a customer-success outreach list. You'd be paging the success team about ghosts.

stages.prompt:
You write:

```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
```

You run it. The new customer Vikram (signed up Monday, zero orders) shows up with `order_count = 1`. **What's wrong?**

options.label: `COUNT(*)` counts the row, including the LEFT JOIN's NULL-filled row. Should be `COUNT(o.id)`.
options.explain: **Sharp.** `COUNT(*)` counts rows; the LEFT JOIN produces one row for Vikram with NULL order columns. `COUNT(o.id)` (or any non-nullable order column) skips NULLs and correctly returns `0`. This is one of the most-failed SQL interview questions.

options.label: The `GROUP BY` is missing `c.signed_up_at`.
options.explain: Not selected, so not required. The bug is `COUNT(*)` vs `COUNT(o.id)`. Look at how COUNT treats NULL.

options.label: Vikram has a hidden order from a test run last week.
options.explain: Possible in real life, but the question is about the query semantics. `COUNT(*)` is the structural cause. Don't blame the data when the query is the bug.

options.label: Should use `COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)` instead.
options.explain: **Also correct.** `COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)` produces the right count *and* protects against accidental fan-out if a future engineer adds another JOIN. Defensive choice. Aunty Lakshmi gives a small nod.

stages.prompt: Aanya looks at the results: *"Wait — the totals don't match the finance dashboard. They say we have 7,200 customers; your query returns 9,800."* What's your **next diagnostic**?

options.label: Check whether `customers` includes soft-deleted (`deleted_at IS NOT NULL`) accounts that finance excludes.
options.explain: **First place to look.** Finance dashboards almost always filter out soft-deleted customers; raw `customers` queries don't. Add `WHERE c.deleted_at IS NULL` and watch the 2,600 ghosts disappear.

options.label: Re-run with `INNER JOIN` to be safe.
options.explain: That would *drop* the zero-order customers Aanya specifically asked for. You'd reduce the count, but for the wrong reason — and break the original requirement. Aunty Lakshmi says: *"Never fix a count by changing the JOIN type without understanding the discrepancy."*

options.label: Check whether the `orders` table is causing fan-out somehow.
options.explain: You're aggregating with `GROUP BY c.id`, so each customer collapses to one row regardless of orders. Fan-out isn't the inflation source here — soft-deletes or test accounts are the usual culprits.

options.label: Add `WHERE c.signed_up_at >= '2024-01-01'` to filter to recent customers.
options.explain: You're guessing at a date filter without knowing what finance does. That's how reports diverge in opposite directions. Find out *why* the gap exists before changing anything.

stages.prompt: You add `WHERE c.deleted_at IS NULL`. Counts now match: 7,200. Final query, ready to ship. **One last polish — what do you add before sending?**

options.label: `ORDER BY order_count DESC, c.signed_up_at DESC` so success can prioritize.
options.explain: **Helpful.** Success will sort the CSV anyway, but pre-sorting by `order_count DESC` puts whales first and `signed_up_at DESC` puts new signups (the zero-order ones success cares about) at the top of *their* section. Two birds.

options.label: A header comment: `-- 7,200 customers · LEFT JOIN orders · excludes soft-deleted · run 2026-05-08`
options.explain: **Excellent practice.** When this CSV gets forwarded three times and someone asks "is this current?" three weeks from now, the comment answers without an email thread.

options.label: `LIMIT 100` to keep it small.
options.explain: Aanya asked for *all* customers. A `LIMIT` would cut off most of the 7,200 — including, ironically, most of the zero-order customers success specifically wanted to find.

options.label: Wrap it in a `SELECT *` outer query for safety.
options.explain: Wrapping a clean query in `SELECT *` undoes everything you just fixed. Aunty Lakshmi looks personally hurt.

outcomes.perfect: Textbook. You picked the right JOIN, caught the `COUNT(*)` trap, diagnosed the soft-delete inflation, and shipped a polished result. **Aunty Lakshmi quietly adds your name to the on-call rotation as a backup — the highest compliment she gives.**
outcomes.good: You shipped a workable query, but you missed at least one of: the `COUNT(*)` NULL-counting trap, the soft-delete diagnostic, or the LEFT vs RIGHT readability call. Re-read the JOIN-direction and `COUNT` sections — these are the everyday traps.
outcomes.learn: Re-read the lesson — especially the **fan-out** section and the discussion of how `COUNT(*)` interacts with `LEFT JOIN`. The query you would have shipped today double-counts revenue and miscounts customers. Aanya's customer-success team would have spent the week chasing customers who don't exist.

points: JOINs are matchmakers — INNER keeps matches only, LEFT keeps the left side intact
Pick the JOIN by intent: what's the unit of work, what should happen to unmatched rows?
Fan-out: when one left row matches many right rows, downstream aggregations double-count
SUM and COUNT(DISTINCT) survive fan-out; AVG of left-side columns does not
Pre-aggregate the right side in a CTE to avoid fan-out entirely; or use COUNT(DISTINCT)

lessons.title: GROUP BY Collapses Reality
lessons.subtitle: Aggregation, HAVING vs WHERE, and the silent-NULL trap

audioChapters.label: Mental model: GROUP BY is a controlled collapse
Move 2 — HAVING vs WHERE — when each runs

blocks.md:
Up to now we've been pulling rows. Most real questions don't want rows — they want *summaries*. *How many customers per city?* *Average order value per product category?* *Cities where total revenue exceeds 10 lakh?*

GROUP BY is the operator that turns many rows into a summary. By the end of this lesson you'll write summaries that count what you actually meant, with HAVING vs WHERE in the right slot, and the silent-NULL trap defused.

blocks.caption: Watch GROUP BY collapse 50 customer rows into 4 city rows, with COUNT/SUM/AVG calculated per group.

blocks.title: Mental model: GROUP BY is a controlled collapse
blocks.md:
GROUP BY tells the database: *first sort all rows into buckets by this column, then collapse each bucket into one row using these aggregate functions.*

The rule that follows: **every column in your SELECT must either be GROUP BY'd or aggregated.** Anything else is ambiguous — *which row's value would I show for this column?* The database refuses to guess.

Most beginner GROUP BY errors are this rule, violated. Once you see it, you can never write a wrong GROUP BY again.

blocks.caption: Animated collapse of 50 rows into 4 groups, with COUNT, SUM, AVG plotted per group.

hi-IN.title: Ration card — GROUP BY HAR ghar ka
hi-IN.md:
Government ration card *one row per HOUSEHOLD* (group), not per person.

Kaise banta hai? **Sab logon ko ghar (group) mein collapse karke** unke total income, total members, total dependents — yahi GROUP BY hai.

Query analogy:
```sql
SELECT household_id, SUM(income) AS total_income
FROM individuals
GROUP BY household_id;
```

Original mein 1.4 billion rows. Output mein ~300 million households. **Yeh collapse hai.**

en.title: The household-vs-individual collapse
en.md: A ration card lists one row per household, not per person. The household_id column is the grouping key; individual incomes are summed; individual names are NOT shown (which person's name would you pick?). GROUP BY is exactly this.

blocks.md:
Five aggregates do 95 percent of the work:

- **COUNT(\*)** — total rows in the group, including rows with NULLs
- **COUNT(col)** — rows in the group where `col` IS NOT NULL
- **SUM(col)** — sum of non-NULL values
- **AVG(col)** — sum / count, ignoring NULLs (which is sometimes what you want, sometimes silently wrong)
- **MIN/MAX(col)** — extremes; ignore NULL

The trap: **COUNT(\*) and COUNT(col) are different.** If `discount` is sometimes NULL, `COUNT(discount)` undercounts vs `COUNT(*)` by exactly the number of NULLs.

blocks.prompt: Run this query, then modify it to also include the count of orders that have a non-NULL coupon_code per city.
blocks.expected:
SELECT city,
  COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
  COUNT(coupon_code) AS coupon_orders,
  SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;
blocks.hint: Add COUNT(coupon_code) to the SELECT — it'll count only rows where coupon_code is not NULL.

blocks.title: Translation moment: 'top 3 cities by orders, but only cities with at least 100 orders'

steps.label: 1. English
steps.body: Top 3 cities by total orders, but only cities with at least 100 orders.

steps.label: 2. The grain
steps.body: We want one row per city. So GROUP BY city.

steps.label: 3. The aggregate
steps.body: Total orders per city — COUNT(*).

steps.label: 4. The post-aggregate filter
steps.body: 'At least 100 orders' is a condition on the aggregate, not the rows. That's HAVING, not WHERE.

steps.label: 5. The full query
steps.body: Sort by count, take 3.
steps.code:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 100
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 3;

blocks.prompt: What's the difference between `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(coupon_code)` when coupon_code is sometimes NULL?

choices.label: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(coupon_code) counts only rows where coupon_code IS NOT NULL
choices.explain: Correct. The difference between them tells you how many rows have a missing coupon.

choices.label: They are identical
choices.explain: Tempting if you've never thought about it; not true. NULL is excluded from COUNT(col).

choices.label: COUNT(*) requires a column argument; COUNT(col) doesn't
choices.explain: Inverse of the truth. COUNT(*) is the no-argument form; COUNT(col) takes a column.

choices.label: COUNT(*) ignores NULLs and COUNT(col) doesn't
choices.explain: Inverted. * ignores nothing; col-form ignores NULL.

hi-IN.title: Yelp average rating — silent NULL ka classic
hi-IN.md:
Restaurant ke pass 5 ratings hain: 5, 5, 5, NULL, NULL. AVG(rating) = (5+5+5)/3 = **5.0**.

Lagta hai *"5 stars!"* — actual mein woh dukan ne 2 logon ko dirty plate diya, woh review skip kar gaye. Real avg: bhul jao.

**AVG silently ignores NULL.** Yelp sample size dikhata hai isi liye — `(based on 3 ratings)`. Tu apne report mein bhi `COUNT(*)` aur `AVG(rating)` saath dikhana — context bina avg meaningless hai.

en.title: AVG silently ignores NULLs
en.md: AVG drops NULL rows. Three perfect ratings + two no-shows = 5.0 average. Always show COUNT alongside AVG so the reader can judge sample size. Yelp does this; you should too.

blocks.text: Move 2 — HAVING vs WHERE — when each runs

blocks.md:
WHERE filters **rows before** the GROUP BY. HAVING filters **groups after** the GROUP BY.

- *I want orders > 1000* → WHERE amount > 1000
- *I want cities with at least 100 orders* → HAVING COUNT(\*) >= 100
- *I want orders > 1000, only from cities with at least 100 such orders* → both: WHERE filters first, HAVING filters the resulting groups

Bugs come from putting the condition in the wrong slot. `WHERE COUNT(*) > 100` is illegal — COUNT doesn't exist yet at that stage. `HAVING amount > 1000` works in some databases but is anti-idiomatic; that's a row filter.

blocks.caption: The pipeline. WHERE runs early, on rows. HAVING runs late, on groups. Putting them in the wrong slot is either an error or a wasted operation.

blocks.title: The classic trap: WHERE on an aggregate
blocks.md:
```sql
-- ❌ This is a syntax error
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
WHERE COUNT(*) >= 100        -- WHERE runs BEFORE COUNT exists
GROUP BY city;
```

The database raises an error here, which is the kind way to fail. The harder bug is when you accidentally pre-filter rows you should have aggregated first:

```sql
-- ❌ Subtle: filters out small orders BEFORE counting
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
WHERE amount > 1000
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 100;
-- This finds cities with at least 100 orders ABOVE 1000.
-- That may or may not be what you wanted. State your intent in a comment.
```

blocks.prompt: Order the SQL execution stages from first to last:

items.label: FROM (which tables, JOINs)
items.detail: Source rows are assembled.

items.label: WHERE (per-row filter)
items.detail: Drop rows that fail the row condition. Aggregates do not exist here yet.

items.label: GROUP BY (collapse)
items.detail: Surviving rows get bucketed; aggregates are computed per bucket.

items.label: HAVING (per-group filter)
items.detail: Drop groups whose aggregate fails the group condition.

items.label: SELECT (pick columns + aggregates to expose)
items.detail: Choose what to project from each surviving group.

items.label: ORDER BY + LIMIT
items.detail: Sort and slice the final result.

blocks.instruction: Write a query that returns each city's total orders, total revenue, and average order amount — but only cities with at least 2 orders. Sort by revenue descending.
blocks.expected:
SELECT city,
  COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
  SUM(amount) AS total_revenue,
  AVG(amount) AS avg_order
FROM orders
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO TRUE statements about GROUP BY:

choices.label: Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY
choices.explain: Correct. Anything else is ambiguous — which row's value would the database show?

choices.label: AVG(col) ignores rows where col IS NULL — always show COUNT alongside
choices.explain: Correct. Without context on sample size, AVG can be silently misleading.

choices.label: WHERE and HAVING are interchangeable
choices.explain: False. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. Different stages.

choices.label: GROUP BY guarantees the result will be sorted by the grouping column
choices.explain: False. GROUP BY does not guarantee order. Use ORDER BY explicitly.

hi-IN.md:
Sochna bahut simple — railway pe imagine kar:

**WHERE** = ticket counter pe filter karna *"sirf 18+ allowed"*. Kuch log andar hi nahi ja sakte.

**HAVING** = train pe board hone ke baad *"sirf coaches jismein 50+ passengers ho"* — pure trains drop ho jaayegi if under-capacity.

en.title: Two filters, two stages
en.md: WHERE is the ticket counter (per-passenger). HAVING is the post-boarding capacity check (per-train). Different stages, different objects, different semantics. Putting one in the other's slot is either a syntax error or a silent wrong answer.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 4.5-Star Product That Wasn't
blocks.source: Anonymous senior data analyst at GharSe, a Hyderabad-based home-services marketplace
blocks.story:
GharSe's Head of Product, on January 17, 2025, opened the weekly product-quality dashboard with a smile: their newly launched **"deep clean — premium"** service had a stellar **4.5-star average** across 800 ratings. He greenlit a ₹1.2 crore marketing push and put it on the homepage hero.

By late February, refund requests for that service spiked 380%. The CX team flagged it. The data team re-ran the rating math, this time *not* trusting the dashboard.

The dashboard query was:

```sql
SELECT service_id, AVG(rating) AS avg_rating
FROM bookings
WHERE service_id = 'deep-clean-premium'
GROUP BY service_id;
```

The gotcha: of the 800 "ratings," only **120 were actual numeric scores**. The other 680 were `NULL` — customers who never opened the rating prompt. `AVG()` silently skips NULLs. The 4.5 was an average of 120 self-selecting happy customers (the 15% who bothered to rate). The other 680 included **a lot of unhappy people** who churned in silence.

When the analyst recalculated treating non-responses as a 1-star equivalent (the conservative business assumption), the rating was **1.8 stars**. The marketing push was paused mid-campaign. The Head of Product wrote a memo titled *"Why I'm never trusting a single AVG() ever again."*

Net cost: ₹47 lakh in spent ad budget on a product that needed fixing first, plus three months of customer trust to repair.
blocks.takeaway: `AVG()`, `SUM()`, `COUNT()` and friends silently skip `NULL` — and the *response rate* is often the most important number on the dashboard.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Quarterly Top-Cities Report
blocks.setup:
Tuesday afternoon. **Aanya, the PM**, pings you on Slack:

*"Hey, can you pull the top 10 cities by revenue for Q1 2026? But only count paid orders. Exclude refunds (negative amounts). And only include cities with at least 3 distinct customers — leadership doesn't want one-customer cities skewing things. Also they want average order size per city. Need it by EOD."*

The schema:

```sql
customers (id, name, city, signed_up_at)
orders    (id, customer_id, amount, status, ordered_at)
-- amount is positive for sales, negative for refunds
-- status is 'paid' | 'pending' | 'cancelled'
```

coach.name: DBA Aunty Lakshmi
coach.role: Senior database administrator, GROUP BY whisperer

stages.prompt: First decision — **where do you put the "at least 3 distinct customers" filter**?

options.label: In the `WHERE` clause: `WHERE COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) >= 3`.
options.explain: `WHERE` runs *before* aggregation, on row-by-row predicates. It cannot reference an aggregate function. The query won't even parse. Aunty Lakshmi: *"WHERE filters rows. HAVING filters groups."*

options.label: In the `HAVING` clause: `HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) >= 3`.
options.explain: **Correct.** `HAVING` runs *after* `GROUP BY` and can reference aggregates. This is the textbook use case: filter groups (cities) based on a property of the group (customer count).

options.label: In the `WHERE` clause as `WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id ...)` somehow.
options.explain: You'd have to write a correlated subquery that re-counts customers per city for every row — possible but absurd. `HAVING` exists exactly so you don't have to do this.

options.label: Run the query first, then filter the result in a spreadsheet.
options.explain: Now the report can't be re-run unattended. Tomorrow's version will silently include one-customer cities again. Always push business rules into the query.

stages.prompt: Where do you handle **"only paid orders, exclude refunds"** — `WHERE` or `HAVING`?

options.label: Both go in `WHERE`: `WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount > 0`.
options.explain: **Right.** Both are row-level predicates — they're true or false for a single order, no aggregation needed. `WHERE` is more efficient because it filters before grouping (less data to aggregate).

options.label: `status = 'paid'` in `WHERE`, but refund exclusion via `HAVING SUM(amount) > 0`.
options.explain: `HAVING SUM(amount) > 0` would let an individual ₹-500 refund row through, then *net* it against positive sales for the city. The city total stays positive but the per-row refunds still inflate `COUNT(*)`. Filter refunds at the row level.

options.label: Both in `HAVING` — safer.
options.explain: You'd be aggregating every row including pending and cancelled orders, then filtering after. Wasted work and risk of including the wrong rows in counts. Aunty Lakshmi: *"Filter early. Aggregate late."*

options.label: Add a `CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN amount ELSE 0 END` instead of filtering.
options.explain: Clever but it leaves the wrong rows in `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)`. A pending-order customer in Pune would still count toward the 3-customer minimum. Filter rows out, don't zero them.

stages.prompt:
You write:

```sql
SELECT c.city,
       SUM(o.amount) AS revenue,
       AVG(o.amount) AS avg_order,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) AS distinct_customers
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  AND o.amount > 0
  AND o.ordered_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31'
GROUP BY c.city
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) >= 3
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Aunty Lakshmi reviews. **What does she flag first?**

options.label: `BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31'` excludes orders placed at 2026-03-31 14:30 if `ordered_at` is a timestamp — should be `< '2026-04-01'`.
options.explain: **Classic.** `BETWEEN` is inclusive on both ends, but `'2026-03-31'` parses as `2026-03-31 00:00:00`. Any order on March 31 after midnight is silently excluded. The half-open form `>= '2026-01-01' AND < '2026-04-01'` is bulletproof and the industry-standard pattern.

options.label: `AVG(o.amount)` should be `SUM(amount) / COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` for "average order size."
options.explain: Read carefully — Aanya asked for *average order size*, not *average per customer*. `AVG(o.amount)` is correct. (If she'd asked "average revenue per customer," you'd be right.) But Aunty Lakshmi nods at the careful reading.

options.label: `GROUP BY c.city` should also include `c.id` for safety.
options.explain: Adding `c.id` would group by *every customer in every city*, giving you per-customer-per-city rows. You'd lose the city-level rollup entirely. The current `GROUP BY` is right.

options.label: Missing `WHERE c.deleted_at IS NULL` to exclude soft-deleted customers.
options.explain: **Good catch.** Soft-deleted customers shouldn't contribute to a top-cities report. Add it. Two-for-the-price-of-one — Aunty Lakshmi awards both points.

stages.prompt: Final ship — Aanya asks one more thing: *"Can you also add a column for the percentage each top-10 city contributes to total Q1 revenue?"* **What's the cleanest way?**

options.label: A window function: `100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER ()` in a wrapping `SELECT`.
options.explain: **Elegant.** Wrap the existing query in a CTE or subquery, then use `SUM(revenue) OVER ()` in the outer `SELECT`. One query, one pass, no joins back to itself. *(Note: this gives % of top-10 revenue, not % of all-cities revenue — clarify with Aanya which she means.)*

options.label: Run a separate query for total Q1 revenue, then divide in code.
options.explain: Two queries, two failure modes, two timestamps that might not match if data updates between them. Use a window function and ship one atomic query.

options.label: Add `AVG(amount) / SUM(amount) * 100` in the SELECT.
options.explain: That math is meaningless — average-order divided by total-revenue isn't a contribution percentage of anything useful. Aunty Lakshmi removes her glasses slowly.

options.label: Tell Aanya it's out of scope and ship the original query.
options.explain: It's a 5-line addition with a window function. Refusing reasonable scope creep that takes 60 seconds is bad partnership. (Refusing scope creep that takes 6 hours is good partnership — know the difference.)

outcomes.perfect: Surgical work. You handled `WHERE` vs `HAVING`, the `BETWEEN`-on-timestamps gotcha, the soft-delete diagnostic, *and* delivered the contribution-percentage ask cleanly. **Aunty Lakshmi sends a thumbs-up GIF. From Aunty Lakshmi, this is effusive praise.**
outcomes.good: You shipped a working report with the right HAVING and the right filters. You missed at least one of: the `BETWEEN`-timestamp trap, the soft-delete filter, or the cleanest way to add the percentage column. Re-read the section on aggregate execution order.
outcomes.learn: Re-read the lesson — especially **`WHERE` vs `HAVING`** (one filters rows, the other filters groups) and the **NULL-handling behavior** of `AVG`/`SUM`/`COUNT`. The query you would have shipped today either won't parse or will silently miscount March 31's orders.

points: GROUP BY is a controlled collapse — buckets rows by a key, then aggregates each bucket
Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY — anything else is ambiguous
COUNT(*) ≠ COUNT(col) when col contains NULLs
AVG silently ignores NULL — always show COUNT alongside AVG so readers can judge
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after — never confuse the two

lessons.title: Subqueries, CTEs, and the Read-Order Lie
lessons.subtitle: How execution order differs from write order, and why CTEs win

audioChapters.label: Mental model: what you write vs what runs
Move 2 — Composing CTEs into a pipeline

blocks.md:
Until now we've written queries small enough that 'what you write' and 'what runs' looked the same. This lesson is the moment they diverge — and the moment SQL becomes a language you can actually compose.

The insight: **SQL's clauses don't run in the order you write them.** Once you see the real order, two things happen. (1) Subqueries stop being mysterious. (2) You discover CTEs and write 30 percent less SQL forever.

blocks.caption: Watch the same query — read order on the left, execution order on the right — light up clause by clause.

blocks.title: Mental model: what you write vs what runs
blocks.md:
Write order:  `SELECT … FROM … WHERE … GROUP BY … HAVING … ORDER BY … LIMIT`.

Execution order:

1. **FROM** + JOINs — assemble source rows
2. **WHERE** — filter rows
3. **GROUP BY** — collapse
4. **HAVING** — filter groups
5. **SELECT** — project columns and aggregates
6. **ORDER BY** — sort
7. **LIMIT** — slice

The SELECT clause runs **second-to-last**, even though you write it first. This is why you can't reference a SELECT alias in WHERE (the alias doesn't exist yet) but you can reference it in ORDER BY (which runs after SELECT).

Commit this order to memory. It explains every 'why won't this work' moment for the next two years.

blocks.caption: A 3-stage CTE pipeline animated: each CTE produces a stage; downstream stages reference upstream ones; final SELECT composes them.

hi-IN.title: Recipe ka 'order of operations' — same trap
hi-IN.md:
Recipe likhi hai *"Tomato chop karke onion ke saath fry karo. Pehle masala bhuna lo."*

Reader sochta hai *"top-to-bottom: tomato chop → onion fry → masala bhun."* Cooking ka order yeh nahi hai. Pehle masala bhun, fir onion fry, fir tomato.

**Read order ≠ execution order.** Recipe likhne wala nayi banane wala nahi tha — woh sochne mein order alag hai, karne mein order alag hai. SQL bhi same hai.

en.title: The recipe-order analogy
en.md: Recipes often read top-to-bottom but instruct the cook to do steps out of order ('first, brown the spice'). The reader has to do the translation. SQL is the same: SELECT comes first in the text, runs second-to-last in execution. Once you see this, debugging gets a lot faster.

blocks.md:
There are three ways to compose queries: subqueries in WHERE/SELECT, derived tables in FROM, and CTEs (`WITH`).

Subqueries in SELECT — *scalar subqueries* — are tempting and almost always a smell:

```sql
-- ❌ Scalar subquery; runs once per row of the outer query
SELECT name,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id) AS order_count
FROM customers c;
```

**CTE form** — same logic, single pass, easier to read, easier to optimize:

```sql
-- ✅ CTE; database can plan and reuse
WITH order_counts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(oc.n, 0) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN order_counts oc ON oc.customer_id = c.id;
```

The rule: **scalar subqueries in SELECT are a code smell — refactor to a CTE + JOIN.** This is one of the few things in SQL where you can take a confident position.

blocks.prompt: Refactor this scalar-subquery version to use a CTE.
blocks.expected:
WITH order_counts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, c.city, COALESCE(oc.n, 0) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN order_counts oc ON oc.customer_id = c.id;

blocks.title: Translation moment: 'top 5 cities by revenue, with average order size, but only Q1 2026 paid orders'

steps.label: 1. English
steps.body: Top 5 cities by revenue in Q1 2026 (paid orders only), with each city's average order size.

steps.label: 2. Stage 1 — Filter to relevant orders
steps.body: Pre-filter; this is the WHERE. CTE makes it reusable.
steps.code:
WITH paid_q1 AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid'
    AND ordered_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31'
)

steps.label: 3. Stage 2 — Aggregate by city
steps.body: Group, sum, average.
steps.code:
, city_totals AS (
  SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS revenue, AVG(amount) AS avg_order
  FROM paid_q1
  GROUP BY city
)

steps.label: 4. Stage 3 — Top 5
steps.body: Sort and slice.
steps.code:
SELECT city, revenue, avg_order
FROM city_totals
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5;

steps.label: 5. The shape
steps.body: Pipeline reads top-to-bottom in the order of the question. No nesting. No re-reading. Reviewers love it; future-you loves it.

blocks.prompt: Why is a scalar subquery in SELECT often a smell?

choices.label: It runs once per row of the outer query unless the planner is clever, hurting performance and obscuring intent
choices.explain: Correct. The CTE form gives the planner more freedom to optimize and is easier to read.

choices.label: Scalar subqueries are not allowed in standard SQL
choices.explain: False; they are valid SQL. They're just usually the wrong tool.

choices.label: They produce wrong answers
choices.explain: Not wrong; just often slower and less readable. Wrong answers come from semantic bugs, not from the scalar-subquery shape itself.

choices.label: They cannot reference outer-query columns
choices.explain: Inverted — they CAN reference outer-query columns (that's what makes them 'correlated'). It's that very correlation that often makes them slow.

hi-IN.title: Nested subqueries — Russian doll trap
hi-IN.md:
Tu likhta hai:
```sql
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT * FROM (
      SELECT * FROM orders
      WHERE amount > 100
    ) sub1
    WHERE city = 'Mumbai'
  ) sub2
  GROUP BY customer_id
) sub3
ORDER BY total DESC;
```

Four levels deep. Bahut clever lag raha hai.

Doosri din wapas dekha — *"yeh main ne kya likha?"*

**CTEs ka use kar.** Same logic, top-to-bottom, har stage ka naam. Reviewer thank kar dega; future-tu bhi.

en.title: The Russian-doll subquery
en.md: Four levels of nested subqueries are clever today and unreadable on Monday. CTEs flatten the same logic into a top-to-bottom pipeline with named stages. Same query plan; vastly better readability.

blocks.text: Move 2 — Compose CTEs into a pipeline

blocks.md:
The real power of CTEs is composition. Each CTE is a named stage. Stages can reference earlier stages. The whole query reads like a pipeline.

This is the shape every senior SQL writer reaches for:

```sql
WITH stage1 AS (...),
     stage2 AS (... FROM stage1 ...),
     stage3 AS (... FROM stage2 ...)
SELECT ... FROM stage3;
```

Review rule: **if you wrote the same subquery twice in the same query, it should be a CTE.** If your nesting is more than two levels deep, it should be a CTE. If a reviewer asks 'what does this part do?', it should be a CTE — *the name of the CTE is the documentation*.

intro: OK final code review of the course. ☕

scenarios.explain: Subquery in WHERE — totally idiomatic. 'IN (subquery)' is one of the cleanest forms in SQL. Don't over-CTE small queries; it adds noise.

scenarios.situation:
```sql
SELECT name,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id) AS n,
  (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id) AS rev
FROM customers c;
```
scenarios.explain: Two scalar subqueries on the same source. Refactor to one CTE (`order_summary` with COUNT and SUM) and LEFT JOIN. Cleaner, faster, easier to extend.

Three levels of nested SELECT *. Refactor each level to a named CTE; or, better, collapse into one query (`SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE amount > 100 AND city = 'Mumbai' GROUP BY customer_id`).

scenarios.situation:
```sql
SELECT city, COUNT(*)
FROM orders
WHERE COUNT(*) > 100
GROUP BY city;
```
scenarios.explain: WHERE on an aggregate — that's invalid SQL because COUNT doesn't exist at WHERE-evaluation time. Block; teach. The fix is `HAVING COUNT(*) > 100`.
Clean two-stage pipeline. CTEs are named (paid_q1, city_rev), no nesting, top-to-bottom flow. Ship as-is; mild nit: replace `SELECT *` in the final SELECT with explicit column list.
